profile.summary: FastSpel predicts the fragment intensities of a tryptic peptide measured by higher-energy collisional dissociation, so that a spectral library can be generated or peptide-spectrum matches rescored. It takes a list of precursors, each with a modified sequence, a precursor charge and a collision energy, and returns the non-zero predicted b and y ion intensities with their m/z values. Instead of a neural network it fits a separate multistep linear regression for each peptide length, charge and collision energy, which makes it fast and its parameters readable.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: For each combination of peptide length, precursor charge and collision energy, FastSpel fits a multistep linear regression that maps a binary encoding of the peptide sequence to the fragment intensity profile. Peptides are built from the 20 common amino acids plus oxidised methionine, so the encoding uses 21 symbols, and fragments are predicted up to charge min(3, precursor charge). The model is effectively hundreds of small separate models: the paper says 350 length, charge and collision energy triplets were trained. Because the relation is linear, the authors read the fitted coefficients and find known fragmentation rules such as the proline effect.

sections.title: How the benchmark used it
sections.body: PepSpecBench calls FastSpel a linear model of about 50K parameters and uses it as a lower-bound reference, with its output projected into the benchmark's shared fragment layout. All six baselines, FastSpel among them, were retrained on the benchmark data under backbone-disjoint splits, so that parameter figure and those results describe the benchmark's retrained model rather than the released package.

strengths.text: Prediction is fast on CPU only: the authors report one million precursors in under 5 s on a single CPU core, and hundreds of times faster than Prosit, PeptDeep and MS2PIP in their own test.

quotes.text: Using a single (AMD EPYC 3.8 GHZ) CPU, FastSpel is able to predict intensities for one million precursors in less than 5 s.
using only 1 CPU, FastSpel is hundreds of times faster than the other three methods

strengths.text: The fitted coefficients can be read directly, and the authors use them to recover known fragmentation rules such as the proline effect.

This simple linear relation allows us to easily interpret the model parameters and relate them to known rules of fragmentation chemistry (e.g., the “proline effect”), or suggest new fragmentation patterns.

strengths.text: Retraining is cheap: the authors say less than 40 s per collision energy, so the method can be refitted for other instruments, CID data or non-tryptic peptides.

quotes.text: This amounts to less than 40 s per collision energy. It is therefore quite fast to retrain FastSpel with more training data, or to train it for more collision energy values, new instruments, CID data, or nontryptic peptides.

run_guide.summary: Download the FastSpel package, install it, and predict fragment intensities for the example precursor list.
prerequisites: Python with pip. numpy, scipy, pandas and h5py are installed with the package.
CPU only: the sources describe prediction on CPU cores and give no GPU requirement.
A precursor list as a comma-separated file with modified_sequence, precursor_charge and collision_energy; an example ships in the package.

notes: FastSpel has a real release of its own, a Python package on the authors' NCBI group site, so no stub was written. There is no code host and no stated licence, so both licence facts are unreported and the source licence field is left off the download page and the FTP listing. context_length is recorded as 30 residues, the top of the trained peptide length range, not an architectural limit. The record's description gives about 50K parameters, which is PepSpecBench's figure for the model it retrained; the model's own sources give no parameter count, so structured.parameters is null.
